title: The Hundred's Sixth Season Ends With New Champions and Old Questions
excerpt: Manchester Super Giants and Trent Rockets won men's and women's titles respectively, but the competition's first fully privatized season has exposed tensions between Indian franchise ambitions and English cricket traditions.
body:
• Manchester Super Giants (men) and Trent Rockets (women) won their first Hundred titles in the competition's sixth season, which ran from July 21 to August 16, 2026
  • Four of eight franchises are now Indian-owned, with the ECB forced to intervene after reports that Indian owners would block Pakistani player signings
  • The season featured rebranded teams, a new player auction model, and an ongoing debate about whether the 100-ball format should convert to T20

The Hundred's sixth season wrapped up on August 16, and if the competition has proved anything across its brief, turbulent history, it is that the gap between commercial ambition and cricketing identity remains stubbornly wide. Manchester Super Giants won the men's title — their first — while Trent Rockets claimed the women's crown, also for the first time, according to the competition's Wikipedia page. Josh Tongue took 14 wickets for the Super Giants, while Annabel Sutherland of Sunrisers Leeds was named women's player of the series with 315 runs.

The Privatization Effect

This was the first season under full private ownership. Six of eight teams were sold to new investors in 2025, with IPL owners acquiring stakes in four franchises: Reliance (MI London, formerly Oval Invincibles), Sun Group (Sunrisers Leeds, formerly Northern Superchargers), Manchester Super Giants (linked to Lucknow Super Giants ownership), and GMR Group (Southern Brave). The total valuation approached £975 million, with over £500 million invested into the English cricket ecosystem, as reported by Sporting News.

https://x.com/OneFootball/status/2089306256808779805

The Wisden Almanack's detailed retrospective on the sale captured a range of stakeholder views. Kavya Maran of Sun Group called the investment "a no-brainer," while broadcaster David Lloyd suggested the competition should expand to 12 teams and convert to T20 entirely.

"Nobody knows when The Hundred will expand, but we must be ready to be part of it."

— Kavya Maran, head of Sun Group, owners of Sunrisers Leeds

The Pakistan Player Controversy

The most politically charged episode of the season emerged before a ball was bowled. Reports indicated that the four Indian-owned franchises would not consider Pakistani players in the pre-season auction. The ECB intervened, with Hundred CEO Vikram Banerjee writing to franchises to insist that "player selection must always be based on cricketing rationale," as reported by Cricbuzz.

The ECB letter, however, exposed its own contradictions. Across the previous five seasons, only two Pakistani players featured in three of those seasons. Not a single Pakistani woman played in any season of the Hundred. In the 2025 draft, no Pakistani player was selected at all — the two who eventually featured came in as injury replacements, according to Cricbuzz's analysis.

Where the Money Leads

The investors secured significant structural concessions, as reported by The Observer. They have a guaranteed window during which the ECB cannot schedule international cricket and have complete control over England-contracted players, who can only be pulled for injury. Investors also secured a veto on any expansion to 10 teams.

London Spirit, despite attracting the largest price tag of all franchises, had a dismal season, with both men's and women's teams eliminated after just six matches. Director of cricket Mo Bobat admitted to "sleepless nights and soul searching," as reported by The Times.

What Comes Next

Expansion remains the elephant in the room. ECB officials have called adding ninth and tenth teams a "no-brainer," with Durham and Bristol considered frontrunner locations. But the existing investors' veto means any growth will require their buy-in — and their commercial calculus, not cricket's developmental needs, will likely drive the timeline.

The deeper question remains whether the 100-ball format itself survives. Multiple voices, including Lloyd and some franchise executives, have suggested converting to T20 to align with the global franchise ecosystem. For now, the Hundred continues in its hybrid form — part IPL satellite, part English experiment, still searching for a stable identity six seasons in.
nri_angle: Four of the eight Hundred franchises are now Indian-owned, making the competition a direct extension of IPL's global ambitions and a new venue for India-Pakistan sporting tensions.
